policylens.title: PolicyLens
policylens.summary: Find the permission that allows a sensitive cloud action, then check whether a proposed correction removes that access.
policylens.imageAlt: Completed PolicyLens sample review showing denied-to-allowed access, source evidence and a candidate correction
policylens.status: Local extension of a public tool
policylens.problem: A policy diff tells a reviewer which JSON changed. PolicyLens evaluates the same sensitive request before and after, cites the granting statement, and checks whether a correction closes that path while preserving required access.
policylens.choice: I kept the permission decision in code. AI receives the checked facts and may explain them, but it cannot overrule the result. This makes a wrong explanation something I can test for, rather than something a reviewer has to guess at.
policylens.result: In the captured local example, deleting a production database changes from denied to allowed. The review identifies the granting statement and checks a candidate correction while preserving required report access.
policylens.learning: A passing test suite only establishes behaviour for the cases it covers. The next useful evidence is comparison with AWS's own simulator, plus adversarial tests of whether AI explanations stay faithful to the engine.
policylens.access: Node.js or Docker. The public example does not need an API key.
policylens.publication: The capture shows the newer local change-review extension. The public repository currently opens the earlier Org demo, not this exact screen.
policylens.mediaCaption: Local change-review example: denied, allowed, then a proposed correction.
steps: Follow the public repository's quick start and open the local app.
Choose Run the 90-second demo to populate the Org view.
Inspect who-can results and their policy citations. The change-review capture above documents a separate, not-yet-published extension.
points: The deterministic engine decides permission reachability. The LLM can explain the result but cannot change it.
The public benchmark and newer local scenario suite are different evidence sets. Neither is a completed independent AWS simulator cross-check.
Run the published benchmark to inspect its documented cases. AI explanations are optional and need a separately configured key.
policylens.note: Local decision support, not an authorization oracle. SCPs, permission boundaries, session policies and some cross-account interactions remain outside the current model.

projectlens.title: ProjectLens
projectlens.summary: Find where a project's written update disagrees with its schedule, then turn the differences into questions for a reviewer.
projectlens.imageAlt: ProjectLens readiness result with three blockers from the synthetic Northstar example
projectlens.problem: A change pack can tell a different story from the Primavera schedule it cites. ProjectLens puts the conflicts beside their source dates before the board decides. The public demo uses static context. Newer local retrieval lets a reviewer inspect cited programme status records; these are not records of past decisions or their causes.
projectlens.choice: I compare the schedule evidence before asking AI for help. Every finding keeps its source dates, and a reviewer must decide whether a suggested precedent is relevant. A plausible narrative is not treated as a project decision.
projectlens.result: The synthetic Northstar example produces three blockers, including a finish date moving by 73 days without being acknowledged. The reviewer can inspect the dates, prepare follow-up questions and export a decision record.
projectlens.learning: The useful output is a question someone can investigate, not a score that pretends to predict project failure. Separating schedule facts from interpretation makes the review easier to challenge.
projectlens.access: Runs in your browser. No account; sample schedules included.
projectlens.publication: The public example uses synthetic schedules. Its precedent cards are a static fallback; live retrieval requires local setup.
projectlens.mediaCaption: Public Northstar sample: three issues to resolve before a decision.
steps: Select Try the Northstar example in the public demo.
Open the three blockers and follow the source dates, including the 73-day movement.
Prepare review questions. Export the record if you want to keep it; the browser is not a shared team workspace.
points: The bundled Northstar schedules are synthetic examples. The browser comparison also accepts your own XER files without uploading them.
The bundled case surfaces three board blockers, including an unacknowledged 73-day finish movement.
Every finding links to schedule evidence and the reviewer records the decision and follow-up.
projectlens.note: Evidence review does not establish contractual entitlement, causation or a probability of failure. The board keeps decision authority.

quicksupply.title: QuickSupply
quicksupply.summary: Follow a school's request for cover through agency assignment and a teacher's response, without losing track of who needs to act next.
quicksupply.problem: A local booking process split same-day cover across dated screens and manual follow-up. QuickSupply separates school, agency and teacher work, then makes each assignment and status handoff visible.
quicksupply.choice: I gave the school, agency and teacher separate views of the same booking. The agency manages offers and exceptions; each role sees its next action instead of editing an undifferentiated list.
quicksupply.result: The recording follows a fictional cover request across the three roles. The shared booking status makes it possible to see whether a request is waiting for assignment or a teacher response.
quicksupply.learning: The product problem was the handoff, not just the appearance of the old screens. A useful next test would observe real school and agency staff handling a declined offer or a last-minute cancellation. This case does not establish adoption or time savings.
quicksupply.access: Watch the recorded prototype without installing anything.
quicksupply.publication: Historical case study with fictional data. The public source is not a deployment-ready staffing service.
quicksupply.mediaCaption: Recorded prototype: school request, agency assignment and teacher response.
steps: The school submits a request for supply cover.
The agency reviews the request and assigns or offers the work to a teacher.
The teacher responds, and the booking status is visible across the separate role views.
points: One request can be followed from school submission through agency assignment to teacher acceptance.
Server-sent events keep the three views in step without manual refresh.
Newer local work adds official DfE vacancy data for aggregate market context. It does not rank teachers and is not part of the published recording.
quicksupply.note: Historical redesign case study, not a live staffing service or a validated startup.

winchester.title: Winchester House Hunter
winchester.summary: Compare a shortlist of homes by budget, station walk and missing evidence, then see what needs checking before a decision.
winchester.imageAlt: Winchester's seeded shortlist with the under £425k filter selected
winchester.problem: A portal listing cannot answer whether one home works for one buyer. House Hunter combines the shortlist with cash position, commute, nearby sold prices, condition notes and next actions.
winchester.choice: I separated the example homes from public completed-sale records, and put missing evidence beside the shortlist. This makes the recommendation a starting point for questions rather than an unexplained ranking.
winchester.result: Choose Under £425k and the nine seeded homes become five. Open Upper Brook Street to inspect the evidence checklist and see which assumptions need checking.
winchester.learning: Precise-looking scores can imply more certainty than the inputs deserve. Fit and evidence scores are demo heuristics, not calibrated probabilities; negotiation figures are illustrative assumptions, not estimated market values.
winchester.access: Runs in your browser. No account; nine seeded homes.
winchester.publication: The public homes, scores and market summaries are illustrative. A local rebuild now traces 931 included 2025 sales to a retained public source, but that provenance update has not been published yet.
winchester.mediaCaption: Public seeded example with the under-£425k filter selected.
steps: Choose Under £425k or a station-distance filter.
Open a home and read its evidence checklist before interpreting the score.
Treat prices and affordability inputs as illustrative. Consult the cited completed-sale context separately.
points: The demo compares nine seeded homes against budget, commute and local completed-sale evidence.
The newer local market build records the HM Land Registry source, filters and reconciled counts. Until that release is public, treat the hosted summaries as illustrative.
The public demo separates seeded homes from completed-sale context and states what it cannot decide.
winchester.note: Illustrative only. Listings and figures are seeded examples, not financial, tax, legal or mortgage advice.

lakehouse.title: Marketing ML Lakehouse
lakehouse.summary: Turn campaign files into checked reporting tables. Explore the public sample, or rebuild the published data pipeline on your computer.
lakehouse.imageAlt: Published lakehouse browser snapshot showing sample quality checks, not a live Python pipeline run
lakehouse.status: Public template with a local ML extension
lakehouse.problem: Before a marketing team acts on a forecast, it needs to know whether the source data is usable and whether the model beats a simple alternative. This reusable local template checks campaign files, keeps a trace of their source, builds analysis tables and tests next-day bookings predictions against carrying today’s figure forward. It is an engineering template, not a connected advertising service.
lakehouse.choice: I made the data rebuildable from files through checked table layers to a dashboard. In the newer local extension, the prediction target is explicitly in the future and the model is compared with carrying today's figure forward.
lakehouse.result: The public browser console shows a fixed quality review with two warnings. The published Python walkthrough rebuilds example tables and a model locally. The newer next-day evaluation is separate local work and is not reproduced by that public walkthrough yet.
lakehouse.learning: A polished forecast is not evidence that a model adds value. Data available only after the prediction time must stay out of training features, and a model needs to beat a simple baseline on later dates before its extra complexity is justified.
lakehouse.access: Browser snapshot needs no setup. Python is required to rebuild the template.
lakehouse.publication: The public console is fixed, and the published model is an earlier example. The prospective next-day evaluation and GA4 adapter are local extensions, not a released public benchmark.
lakehouse.mediaCaption: Fixed public data-quality snapshot, not a live Python pipeline run.
steps: Open Data quality in the public browser snapshot and inspect its warnings.
Use the published DEMO.md to install, rebuild and open the local Streamlit dashboard.
Treat the model as an engineering example. The newer next-day baseline comparison described here is not yet in the published walkthrough.
points: The published Makefile rebuilds DuckDB tables, trains an example model and opens a local Streamlit dashboard.
Local follow-on work adds source checksums, duplicate detection and a future target with a persistence baseline.
A local GA4 adapter explores the same task with public ecommerce data; it is not evidence of results for a connected advertising account.
lakehouse.note: The public console is a fixed sample snapshot, not a live view of the current Python output. Rebuild and inspect your own output in the local Streamlit dashboard. Neither route establishes results for a connected advertising account.

hr.title: HR Performance Analytics
hr.summary: A Power BI case study about why checking the meaning of a field matters as much as building the dashboard.
hr.imageAlt: Historical HR dashboard; its absence and age labels are not reliable interpretations of the source data
hr.status: Historical dashboard; corrected data rebuilt locally
hr.problem: A dashboard screenshot hides the model, calculations and interpretation choices. This case puts the historical AdventureWorks dashboard beside two errors in how I interpreted its fields. Both need correcting before the report can be reused.
hr.choice: The original dashboard made two unsupported interpretations. SickLeaveHours is an available balance, not absence taken. ModifiedDate records when a row changed; it cannot stand in for a birth date or hire date. I am retaining the original work with this correction rather than presenting it as reliable employee analysis.
hr.result: The new local rebuild produces checked CSVs and a corrected review PDF from Microsoft's public sample. Its three available-leave balance bands reconcile to 290 fictional employees. The screenshots here still show the historical dashboard; the original Power BI model has not been refreshed.
hr.learning: A chart can be technically well built and still answer the wrong question. Field definitions, measure assumptions and a correction trail are part of the deliverable, not documentation to add after the visual design.
hr.access: Read the correction here. Power BI Desktop is needed to edit the historical report.
hr.publication: The corrected data and replacement review PDF are local, unpublished work. The public repository still contains historical interpretations. Refreshing and checking the original Power BI report remains outstanding.
hr.mediaCaption: Historical output retained for the case study; labels have not been corrected in the export.
steps: Read the two field-meaning corrections on this page.
Inspect the original exports as historical artefacts, not current HR findings.
Before reuse, rebuild the measures from documented field definitions and validate the resulting PBIX/PDF.
points: Do not label a sick-leave balance as annual absence or use it to identify high-absence employees.
Use appropriate birth and hire dates for age or tenure, not the row's ModifiedDate.
A package validator can check that files exist; it cannot establish that the report's interpretation is correct.
hr.note: Fictional AdventureWorks data, not employee-performance evidence. The historical exports must not inform HR decisions.

england.title: Can England Win It?
england.summary: A one-day World Cup scenario simulator kept as an example of interactive modelling and animation.
england.imageAlt: Can England Win It scenario simulator
england.problem: I wanted to make a small simulation people could play with, rather than present a single opaque football prediction. The result is a deliberately time-bounded experiment in modelling assumptions and animated interaction.
england.choice: I exposed the assumptions and used seeded simulations so the same inputs can be repeated. The animation turns a modelling exercise into something a nontechnical visitor can explore.
england.result: Choose the scenario assumptions and play the tournament to see the simulated outcomes change. The archived model remains interactive; its results are illustrative, not a forecast for a current competition.
england.learning: This was a useful way to practise reproducibility and frontend storytelling in a small build. Finishing the experiment and documenting its assumptions is more honest than treating an event-specific toy as an ongoing product.
england.access: Runs in your browser. No account or setup.
england.publication: Finished entertainment experiment. Assumptions such as player boosts are part of the game, not validated sporting effects.
england.mediaCaption: Recorded scenario simulation from the finished experiment.
steps: Choose the team's mood and pressure response in the public experiment.
Pick a player and play through the simulated tournament.
Change one assumption and compare the scenario, without treating the output as betting guidance.
points: The assumptions stay visible and editable.
Tests cover seeded output, bounds, monotonicity and uncertainty ranges.
The postmortem records what the one-day build achieved and why it stopped.
england.note: A scenario tool for fun, not a forecast or betting product.
